implementations.name: nanopb
notes: nanopb 0.4.9.2 runtime (pb_common.c, pb_encode.c, pb_decode.c) compiled from the pinned release tarball together with the generated bench.pb.c; code generated by the bundled nanopb_generator.py. The generator compiles bench.proto with the protoc bundled in grpcio-tools (libprotoc 35.1), not with $PROTOC 36.2: it offers no option to select a protoc binary. It consumes only the FileDescriptorSet, which is identical for this proto3 file.

Dynamic allocation mode: compiled with PB_ENABLE_MALLOC and every string/bytes/repeated field (including the repeated map-entry fields that represent map<K,V>) is declared type:FT_POINTER in bench.options, so decoding malloc()s/realloc()s like the other libraries and no array size is hard-coded. nanopb's embedded default (static fixed-size fields or callbacks) is not benchmarked.
Compiled with PB_FIELD_32BIT because the 16-bit default pb_size_t (max 65535) cannot hold the 64 KiB (65536 B) bytes blob of the large dataset.
wire_decode: pb_decode from pb_istream_from_buffer into a stack struct followed by pb_release inside the timed iteration.
wire_encode: pb_get_encoded_size (a sizing pass) + malloc + pb_encode into pb_ostream_from_buffer + free per iteration.
JSON operations are unsupported: nanopb has no JSON (ProtoJSON) support.
Maps are represented as repeated entry messages, so re-encoding preserves the fixture entry order and the output is byte-identical to the fixture.

implementations.name: protobuf-c
notes: Generated code from protoc-gen-c; runtime libprotobuf-c linked via pkg-config. The distribution packages are used (1.4.x on the Ubuntu 24.04 Docker image) because protobuf-c 1.5.2 protoc-gen-c does not compile against libprotobuf >= 30; the generated code and C runtime are unaffected by the libprotobuf version.

The pack/unpack hot path lives in the distribution's libprotobuf-c shared library, compiled by Ubuntu with -O2 -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3; only bench.c and the generated descriptor tables are compiled with -O3 by this harness. The other C/C++ runtimes in the suite are built from source with -O3.
wire_decode: <msg>__unpack(NULL, len, data) with the default system allocator, followed by <msg>__free_unpacked inside the timed iteration.
wire_encode: <msg>__get_packed_size + malloc + <msg>__pack + free per iteration (protobuf-c has no sizing-free serialise API).
JSON operations are unsupported: protobuf-c has no JSON (ProtoJSON) support.
Maps are represented as repeated entry messages, so re-encoding preserves the fixture entry order and the output is byte-identical to the fixture.

implementations.name: protobuf
notes: Google's reference C++ runtime (full libprotobuf, not lite, because the JSON util needs descriptors/reflection) linked against the installed 36.2 libraries via find_package(protobuf CONFIG); generated code from protoc --cpp_out with optimize_for = SPEED.

No arenas: wire_decode and json_decode construct a fresh message on the stack per iteration and destroy it at the end of the iteration; wire_encode and json_encode produce a fresh std::string per iteration.

JSON via google/protobuf/util/json_util.h (MessageToJsonString / JsonStringToMessage) with default options, i.e. canonical ProtoJSON. json_util is reflection-driven (it walks descriptors), not generated code; libprotobuf offers no generated JSON path.

Map fields serialise in the runtime's hash-map iteration order, so re-encoded medium/large output is not byte-identical to the fixture (wire_bytes_match=false, wire_size_match=true); the JSON round-trip check therefore compares sizes for those datasets.
library_version is google::protobuf::internal::VersionString(GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_VERSION) of the linked runtime; build/version.txt is the CMake package version.

implementations.name: google-protobuf
notes: Official Google.Protobuf runtime (NuGet) with protoc --csharp_out generated code.
wire_decode = SmallMessage.Parser.ParseFrom(byte[]); wire_encode = msg.ToByteArray().

json_encode = JsonFormatter.Default.Format(msg); json_decode = JsonParser.Default.Parse<T>(string). The output is canonical ProtoJSON but not compact: JsonFormatter.Default emits a space after ':' and ',', so json_encode writes about 10% more bytes than the compact fixture (141/9035/1979535 vs 126/8283/1750634 for small/medium/large). JsonFormatter/JsonParser are reflection-based (descriptor + IFieldAccessor); Google.Protobuf offers no generated JSON code.
Built with dotnet build -c Release, workstation (non-server) GC, default TieredPGO, InvariantGlobalization. TargetFramework net8.0 with RollForward=Major so a newer runtime can execute it.

implementations.name: protobuf-net
notes: Contract classes generated from bench.proto with protobuf-net's own generator (protobuf-net.Protogen dotnet tool, default options). Generated contracts use packed arrays, ZigZag/FixedSize DataFormat, ProtoMap and a DiscriminatedUnion for the oneof; wire output is byte-identical to the fixtures.
wire_decode = Serializer.Deserialize<T>(ReadOnlyMemory<byte>) (allocates a new object graph per iteration).

wire_encode = new MemoryStream(); Serializer.Serialize(ms, msg); ms.ToArray() -- the common user pattern; this includes one extra copy (MemoryStream growth + ToArray) compared to Serializer.Measure/IBufferWriter, which is what users typically pay.
json_encode/json_decode unsupported: protobuf-net has no canonical ProtoJSON support (its contracts can be fed to System.Text.Json/Newtonsoft, but that is not the ProtoJSON mapping).
protobuf-net compiles its serializers at first use (RuntimeTypeModel auto-compile); this happens during calibration/warm-up, not in the timed rounds.
Built with dotnet build -c Release, workstation (non-server) GC, default TieredPGO, InvariantGlobalization. TargetFramework net8.0 with RollForward=Major so a newer runtime can execute it.

implementations.name: protobuf-go
notes: Official google.golang.org/protobuf runtime with protoc-gen-go generated code (same version as the runtime, installed by build.sh into build/bin).
wire_decode = proto.Unmarshal(b, &bench.T{}); wire_encode = proto.Marshal(m) with default MarshalOptions (not Deterministic).

json_encode = protojson.Marshal(m) (default options: compact canonical ProtoJSON); json_decode = protojson.Unmarshal(jsonBytes, &bench.T{}) with the fixture JSON read once as []byte. protojson is reflection-based (protoreflect); protobuf-go offers no generated JSON code.

protojson deliberately injects a per-binary random choice of whitespace after ',' and ':' (internal/detrand), so json_bytes can be slightly larger than a strictly compact encoding and the byte-exact output differs between builds.
Map iteration order in Go is randomised, so wire_bytes_match is expected to be false for medium/large (wire_size_match is what is checked).
Built with plain `go build` (default optimisation, no -race, no PGO).

implementations.name: vtprotobuf
notes: planetscale/vtprotobuf generated fast paths (protoc-gen-go-vtproto features=marshal+unmarshal+size) on top of protoc-gen-go message types from google.golang.org/protobuf.
wire_decode = (&bench.T{}).UnmarshalVT(b); wire_encode = m.MarshalVT(). No pooling (features=pool) and no unsafe features are enabled.

JSON ops use protojson from google.golang.org/protobuf (shared with protobuf-go): vtprotobuf has no JSON support of its own, so the json_encode/json_decode columns measure protojson (reflection-based) and are expected to equal protobuf-go's; they are shown for completeness. json_encode = protojson.Marshal(m); json_decode = protojson.Unmarshal(jsonBytes, &bench.T{}).
protojson deliberately injects a per-binary random choice of whitespace after ',' and ':' (internal/detrand), so json_bytes can be slightly larger than a strictly compact encoding.
Map iteration order in Go is randomised, so wire_bytes_match is expected to be false for medium/large (wire_size_match is what is checked).
Reported version is the vtprotobuf module version; the underlying google.golang.org/protobuf version is pinned in go.mod.

implementations.name: goose-protobuf
notes: goose-protobuf 0.1.0-dev at commit a9e99bb (pinned, the project has no release tag yet; override with GOOSE_PROTOBUF_REF) with protoc-gen-goose generated code, Goose v2026.3. The library is pre-1.0 and describes itself as an experiment; it is included by request, not by the popularity criterion of docs/implementations.md.

Build: goose build at its defaults (no --debug). Goose compiles to C and runs the system C compiler at -O2, generic x86-64, no -march=native; -O2 is the highest level goose build offers, whereas the other C/C++ harnesses compile with -O3. Goose's bounds checks stay on except where its compiler proves them redundant, as in any goose build.

wire_decode: a new local message, M_decode(bytes, m), then M_clear(m), all inside the timed iteration. Messages and their contents live in global per-type pools: this is the library's only memory model, so M_clear hands storage back to pools that the next iteration reuses, and the rule against object pools cannot be applied to this column.

wire_encode: a new local u8[>..] per iteration, M_encode(m, out), no pre-sizing with M_size_of. A local growable array lives on Goose's data stack: it grows in place without moving and is released by resetting the stack top, so there is no malloc or free per iteration. That is how the language allocates, not a harness optimisation.
JSON operations are unsupported: goose-protobuf has no JSON (ProtoJSON) support (binary wire format only).
wire_bytes_match is true for all three datasets: fields and map entries are written in the fixture's order.

Build: build.sh checks out the pinned commit with git, builds the plugin from that checkout, generates bench.goose with $PROTOC and vendors the pb_wire runtime with the project's scripts/vendor_runtime.sh; generated code only builds against the runtime of the same commit. Everything stays under build/, including GOOSE_HOME.

implementations.name: protobuf-java
notes: Official Java runtime (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java) with protoc-generated code (optimize_for = SPEED, java_multiple_files).

wire_decode = SmallMessage.parseFrom(byte[]); wire_encode = msg.toByteArray(). A new message / byte[] is allocated per iteration. wire_encode calls toByteArray() on the shared immutable fixture message, so protobuf-java's memoizedSize makes the size pass run once; other libraries recompute the size every call. This is the idiomatic path (a real user re-serialising the same message object gets the same benefit) and is left as is.

JSON via protobuf-java-util JsonFormat: printer().omittingInsignificantWhitespace().print(msg) and parser().merge(text, builder).build(). The Printer and Parser instances are created once and reused (they are immutable and thread-safe; this is the documented usage). JsonFormat is descriptor-driven (reflective) because protobuf-java offers no generated JSON code path.
Default HotSpot JIT flags (no -XX tuning). Timer: System.nanoTime(). Black hole: static volatile long xor-folded every iteration.
Build: Maven, release 21; runtime jars are resolved by Maven and listed in build/classpath.txt.
implementations.runtime: OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 21.0.12.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu (G1 Young Generation/G1 Concurrent GC/G1 Old Generation, 3 cpus)

implementations.name: wire
notes: Square Wire with Java code generation (wire-compiler --java_out; the wire-maven-plugin only exists for Wire 3.x, so build.sh fetches the pinned wire-compiler jar-with-dependencies from Maven Central and runs it). Runtime: com.squareup.wire:wire-runtime-jvm (Kotlin runtime, Java generated classes).

Generated classes are immutable with public final fields and a Builder; repeated fields are java.util.List, maps are java.util.Map, bytes are okio.ByteString; proto3 singular scalars are primitives (OMIT_IDENTITY).

wire_decode = SmallMessage.ADAPTER.decode(byte[]); wire_encode = SmallMessage.ADAPTER.encode(msg) (returns a new byte[]). A new message / byte[] is allocated per iteration. ADAPTER.encode(msg) writes into an okio Buffer and copies it out with readByteArray(); ADAPTER.decode(byte[]) wraps the input in a Buffer first, so each wire op pays one extra copy of the payload compared with libraries that write straight into a byte[].

JSON via wire-moshi-adapter: Moshi.Builder().add(new WireJsonAdapterFactory()).build() and moshi.adapter(SmallMessage.class) created once and reused; json_encode = adapter.toJson(msg), json_decode = adapter.fromJson(text). Output verified to be the canonical proto3 JSON mapping (lowerCamelCase keys, 64-bit ints as strings, enums as names, bytes as base64, defaults omitted) and semantically identical to the fixture JSON for all three datasets.

wire_bytes_match is false for the medium dataset only because Wire emits oneof members after all other fields (card_token, tag 7, is written after fixed64 checksum, tag 15); the output has identical length and content, just a different field order, and the JSON round-trip check passes on length.
Default HotSpot JIT flags (no -XX tuning). Timer: System.nanoTime(). Black hole: static volatile long xor-folded every iteration.

Build: Maven, release 21; runtime jars are resolved by Maven and listed in build/classpath.txt. The library version is read from pom.xml into build/version.txt and passed to the harness as a system property (Wire has no runtime version API).
implementations.runtime: OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 21.0.12.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu (G1 Young Generation/G1 Concurrent GC/G1 Old Generation, 3 cpus)

implementations.name: protobuf-es
notes: @bufbuild/protobuf v2 runtime with protoc-gen-es generated schemas (target=js+dts). Message objects are plain objects created from the generated schema descriptors (the library's only API; there is no alternative static codegen).
wire_decode = fromBinary(TSchema, bytes); wire_encode = toBinary(TSchema, msg); json_encode = toJsonString(TSchema, msg); json_decode = fromJsonString(TSchema, text). All with default options.
fromBinary bytes fields are zero-copy: decoding returns subarray views of the input buffer (the 64 KiB blob of large is not copied), whereas most other runtimes copy bytes fields into a new buffer.
64-bit integers are bigint; the black hole folds the low 32 bits of created_at.
Map entries are emitted in JavaScript object-key order (integer-like keys ascending), so wire_bytes_match can be false for the datasets with maps while wire_size_match holds.
@bufbuild/protoc-gen-es is pinned to the same version as the runtime in package.json / package-lock.json.

float (32-bit) fields are serialised by JSON.stringify as the exact double value of the float32 (e.g. 575.22 -> 575.219970703125), as both JavaScript libraries do; the values round-trip exactly but json_bytes for the large dataset is ~18% larger than the shortest-repr output of the Go/Python harnesses.

implementations.name: protobufjs
notes: protobuf.js 8.x with pbjs static-module codegen (-t static-module -w esm, protobufjs/minimal runtime): wire_decode = T.decode(buf); wire_encode = T.encode(msg).finish(). No reflection on the wire path.

JSON ops use the official optional ProtoJSON extension protobufjs/ext/protojson (toJsonString / fromJsonString), which is the library's only spec-compliant ProtoJSON implementation (int64 as strings, enums as names, lowerCamelCase, defaults omitted, conformance-tested). It is reflection-driven by design: pbjs has no static-module codegen for ProtoJSON, so the reflected types are loaded once at start-up from a JSON descriptor (pbjs -t json) and the static message objects are passed to it. json_decode therefore yields reflected message instances (same shape/fields as the static ones).
T.decode bytes fields are zero-copy: returns subarray views of the input buffer (the 64 KiB blob of large is not copied), whereas most other runtimes copy bytes fields into a new buffer.
64-bit integers are Long objects (the `long` package is a dependency of protobufjs 8); the black hole folds the low 32 bits of created_at.
Map entries are emitted in JavaScript object-key order (integer-like keys ascending), so wire_bytes_match can be false for the datasets with maps while wire_size_match holds.
pbjs was run with --no-verify --no-delimited --no-typeurl only to trim unused generated helpers; the encode/decode code is unchanged.

float (32-bit) fields are serialised by JSON.stringify as the exact double value of the float32 (e.g. 575.22 -> 575.219970703125), as both JavaScript libraries do; the values round-trip exactly but json_bytes for the large dataset is ~18% larger than the shortest-repr output of the Go/Python harnesses.

implementations.name: protobuf
notes: Official runtime with the upb C backend (PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=upb).

JSON via google.protobuf.json_format (MessageToJson(msg, indent=None) / Parse). json_format is pure Python walking descriptors plus json.dumps/json.loads, all inside the timed region; there is no generated JSON code.
MessageToJson emits ': ' and ', ' separators, so json_bytes is 139/8865/1950193 for small/medium/large against the compact fixture's 126/8283/1750634; the content is canonical ProtoJSON.
Map iteration order follows the upb map, so wire_bytes_match is false for medium/large while wire_size_match holds and the messages are equal.

implementations.name: prost
notes: prost with prost-build generated structs (default settings: HashMap maps, Vec<u8> bytes, String strings).
Wire: Message::decode(&[u8]) / Message::encode_to_vec() allocate a new message / Vec per iteration.

prost has no JSON support itself; JSON uses pbjson + pbjson-build generated serde impls (canonical ProtoJSON: lowerCamelCase, 64-bit ints as strings, enums as names, bytes as base64, defaults omitted) driven by serde_json::to_string / serde_json::from_str.
Map iteration order of HashMap is unspecified, so wire_bytes_match may be false for datasets with maps (medium, large); sizes still match.
Build: cargo build --release --locked with the default release profile (no LTO / PGO / target-cpu).

implementations.name: rust-protobuf
notes: rust-protobuf 3.x (crate `protobuf`, stepancheg) with protobuf-codegen generated structs (protoc backend, default settings: HashMap maps, Vec<u8> bytes, String strings).
Wire: Message::parse_from_bytes / Message::write_to_bytes allocate a new message / Vec per iteration.

JSON via protobuf-json-mapping (print_to_string / parse_from_str), the only JSON path the library offers; it works through the generated static reflection tables rather than generated per-message JSON code.

protobuf-json-mapping has no compact-output option: print_to_string always emits ": " and ", " separators, so json_bytes is ~10% larger than the whitespace-free reference JSON (content is otherwise identical canonical ProtoJSON).
Map iteration order of HashMap is unspecified, so wire_bytes_match may be false for datasets with maps (medium, large); sizes still match.
Build: cargo build --release --locked with the default release profile (no LTO / PGO / target-cpu).

implementations.name: swift-protobuf
notes: apple/swift-protobuf with protoc-gen-swift generated structs (Visibility=Internal); built with swift build -c release (SwiftPM default release settings, no -Ounchecked / cross-module optimisation flags beyond the default).

Wire: Message(serializedBytes: [UInt8]) / serializedBytes() -> [UInt8] (the generic ContiguousBytes API; the fixture is read once into a [UInt8]). A new message value / byte array is created and dropped per iteration (ARC release is part of the iteration).
JSON: jsonString() / Message(jsonString:) with default options (canonical ProtoJSON: lowerCamelCase, 64-bit ints as strings, enums as names, bytes as base64, defaults omitted).
Timer: clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) via Glibc.
Map iteration order of Swift Dictionary is unspecified, so wire_bytes_match may be false for datasets with maps (medium, large); sizes still match.
build.sh builds the protoc-gen-swift plugin from the same pinned package (harness/Package.resolved) and generates into harness/Sources/bench/gen; SwiftPM scratch dir is build/spm.

The SwiftPM package lives in harness/ rather than in this directory: SwiftPM derives the root package identity from the directory name, and 'swift-protobuf' collides with the dependency's identity (SwiftPM silently drops the dependency at resolve time and reports a cyclic dependency at build time).
harness.runtime / library_version are passed to the binary by run.sh from build/runtime.txt (swift --version) and build/version.txt (Package.resolved pin).

implementations.name: zig-protobuf
notes: zig-protobuf 7.0.0 at commit 8033e1e (pinned; override with ZIG_PROTOBUF_REF) with protoc-gen-zig generated structs; built with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=baseline (generic x86-64, matching the other compilers' default targets; Zig would otherwise target the host CPU), no libc.

Allocator: std.heap.smp_allocator (Zig's general purpose allocator for release builds). Every iteration allocates a new message / buffer from it and frees it (msg.deinit, Writer.Allocating.deinit, allocator.free) inside the timed loop; no arena, no reuse.
wire_decode: Msg.decode(&std.Io.Reader.fixed(bytes), allocator); wire_encode: msg.encode(&std.Io.Writer.Allocating, allocator).

wire_encode: the library's writeSubmessage encodes every nested message into a temporary Allocating writer and then copies it into the parent (one alloc + copy + free per submessage; about 15k on large). Much of the gpa column's wire_encode cost is this allocator traffic, which is why the arena/fba variants gain most there.

json_encode: msg.jsonEncode(.{}, .{ .emit_oneof_field_name = false }, allocator). The library default emit_oneof_field_name=true wraps oneof members in an object named after the oneof (a legacy, non-ProtoJSON format), so it is turned off for the canonical mapping.

json_decode: Msg.jsonDecode(text, .{}, allocator), which is std.json.parseFromSlice under the hood: the library allocates the decoded message in a std.json.Parsed arena (owned by the call, freed by parsed.deinit()); there is no non-arena JSON decode API.

wire_bytes_match is false for medium (sizes match, messages are equal): the encoder writes fields in generated-struct order, which places the oneof (fields 7-9) after field 15, so the field order differs from the fixture. Maps are kept as ordered entry lists, so map order is preserved.

The JSON encoder prints float (32-bit) fields with the shortest representation of their f64 widening (e.g. 575.22f -> 575.219970703125), so json_bytes for large is ~18% larger than the reference; the values parse back to identical messages.

The sibling directories zig/zig-protobuf-arena and zig/zig-protobuf-fba run bench-arena / bench-fba from this same build (same sources, one zig build) with an arena or fixed-buffer allocator reset per iteration instead of individual frees; zig/zig-protobuf-native, -arena-native and -fba-native run the same three strategies compiled for the host CPU instead of the x86-64 baseline (bench-native, bench-arena-native, bench-fba-native).

Build: the package is pinned by content hash in build.zig.zon and build.sh checks out the pinned commit (or $ZIG_PROTOBUF_REF when set) with git, feeds it to zig fetch as a local directory (Zig's HTTP client cannot use MITM proxies) and only rewrites the url/hash in build.zig.zon, with a warning, when another ref is requested. protoc from $PROTOC is passed via -Dprotoc; zig-protobuf still requests its own protoc 36.2 archive as a lazy dependency, which build.sh seeds into the package cache.

implementations.name: zig-protobuf
notes: Allocation-strategy variant of zig/zig-protobuf: same library, generated code, harness and build flags (ReleaseFast, -Dcpu=baseline, no libc); only the allocator handed to the library differs.

Allocator: std.heap.ArenaAllocator backed by std.heap.page_allocator, created once per dataset. Every iteration allocates its message / buffer from the arena and ends with arena.reset(.retain_capacity): nothing is freed individually (no msg.deinit, no Allocating.deinit, no free) and the arena keeps its memory, so after the first iterations no call reaches the OS.

This deliberately breaks the suite-wide 'fresh allocation, individual release per iteration' rule (docs/METHODOLOGY.md): the column shows what zig-protobuf costs when the caller owns an arena, not a like-for-like comparison with the other libraries' default columns.

json_decode: zig-protobuf has no leaky JSON decode API (Msg.jsonDecode wraps std.json.parseFromSlice and returns a std.json.Parsed with its own arena), so this variant calls the equivalent std.json.parseFromSliceLeaky(Msg, arena, text, .{}) directly; the generated jsonParse code is the same.
Everything else (JSON options, validation, field-order and float-formatting caveats) is identical to zig/zig-protobuf.
implementations.runtime: Zig 0.17.1 (fast, cpu x86_64 = baseline, std.heap.ArenaAllocator reset per iteration)

implementations.name: zig-protobuf
notes: CPU-target variant: the very same zig-protobuf commit, generated code, harness and ReleaseFast build as zig/zig-protobuf-arena, but compiled for the host CPU (zig's default target; no -Dcpu=baseline) so the compiler may use every instruction set the machine has (AVX2/BMI on x86-64). Every other implementation in the suite, including zig/zig-protobuf-arena, is built for the generic x86-64 baseline, so this column is not like-for-like: it shows what zig-protobuf gains from host-specific code generation, not a comparison with the other libraries.

Allocator identical to zig/zig-protobuf-arena: std.heap.ArenaAllocator reset with .retain_capacity after every iteration, nothing freed individually. This variant therefore combines both deviations from the suite rules (arena allocation and host-specific code) and is an upper bound for zig-protobuf on this machine, not a comparison with the other libraries.
The CPU model the binary was compiled for is reported in harness.runtime (builtin.cpu.model.name), so results from different hosts can be told apart.
Built by the shared zig/zig-protobuf build (one zig build produces all six executables); this directory only runs build/bin/bench-arena-native.
implementations.runtime: Zig 0.17.1 (fast, cpu skylake = host, std.heap.ArenaAllocator reset per iteration)

implementations.name: zig-protobuf
notes: Allocation-strategy variant of zig/zig-protobuf: same library, generated code, harness and build flags (ReleaseFast, -Dcpu=baseline, no libc); only the allocator handed to the library differs.

Allocator: std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator over one 128 MiB slab obtained once from std.heap.page_allocator (pages are touched on first use). Every iteration allocates its message / buffer from the slab and ends with fba.reset(): nothing is freed individually (no msg.deinit, no Allocating.deinit, no free). Growing buffers (encoders, repeated fields) can only be resized in place when they are the last allocation; otherwise a new block is bumped and the data copied, which is why the peak usage (printed in the run log) exceeds the output size.

This deliberately breaks the suite-wide 'fresh allocation, individual release per iteration' rule (docs/METHODOLOGY.md): the column shows the library's cost with a bump allocator and zero deallocation work, an upper bound rather than a like-for-like comparison with the other libraries' default columns.

json_decode: zig-protobuf has no leaky JSON decode API (Msg.jsonDecode wraps std.json.parseFromSlice and returns a std.json.Parsed with its own arena), so this variant calls the equivalent std.json.parseFromSliceLeaky(Msg, fba, text, .{}) directly; the generated jsonParse code is the same.
Everything else (JSON options, validation, field-order and float-formatting caveats) is identical to zig/zig-protobuf.
